articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: A chemical produced by gut bacteria may accelerate Alzheimer’s disease
articles.summary: A metabolic byproduct of gut bacteria can damage the blood-brain barrier and drive the formation of Alzheimer's-related proteins. Elevated levels of the chemical correlate with worse cognitive decline in humans and accelerate neurodegeneration in animal models.

articles.title: People who worry more tend to have more negative dreams, study finds
articles.summary: People who reported more worry and depressive symptoms also tended to report more negative dreams, according to a network analysis of 389 Italian adults that placed stress at the center of daytime distress.

articles.title: How extreme boredom can push people toward aggressive behavior
articles.summary: Boredom does more than just drain your energy. New research reveals that extreme monotony increases the desire for stimulation, pushing people toward both physical aggression and stronger support for military conflicts as a way to escape the dullness.

articles.title: Antidepressants in pregnancy not tied to extra autism or ADHD risk beyond maternal depression, study finds
articles.summary: In a study of more than 167,000 children in Wales, autism and ADHD rates were similar whether a mother’s depression was treated with antidepressants or left untreated. Depression itself, however, was linked to more special educational needs.

articles.title: Women on hormonal birth control view their romantic traits more positively
articles.summary: While hormonal birth control is known to suppress fertility, a series of new psychological evaluations suggests that synthetic hormones may inadvertently boost how women perceive their own romantic desirability, social reputation, and overall value to potential partners.

articles.title: Nearly 30,000 people tested quit-smoking methods. One stood out
articles.summary: Nicotine e-cigarettes appear to help more smokers quit than patches, gum, and several other common approaches, according to a major review of 80 clinical trials. Researchers say regulated vaping products are not risk-free, but may be a significantly less harmful alternative for people who would otherwise continue smoking.

articles.title: Where you direct your attention may shape your body’s inflammatory response
articles.summary: Inflammation is thought to run on autopilot, but new experiments suggest attention plays a role. When people focused on an itchy skin reaction instead of distracting themselves, the swelling was smaller, a pattern seen in about 90 percent of participants.

articles.title: Psychologists map the emotional borders between social anxiety and narcissism
articles.summary: While social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism both stem from feelings of inadequacy, a new study reveals they are driven by different types of shame. Social anxiety relies on self-criticism, whereas narcissism involves a broader fear of outside judgment.

articles.title: Most long-term singles stay satisfied with their lives over 11 years, study finds
articles.summary: Are people who stay single doomed to unhappiness? An 11-year study of German singles suggests not: about 90 percent maintained relatively high life satisfaction, even though their sex lives, desire for a partner, and feelings about being single varied widely.

articles.title: Scientists created a tiny device that can control your nerves to treat chronic pain
articles.summary: Scientists have developed a tiny, injectable device that can control nerve activity without surgery, batteries, or wires, potentially transforming treatment for chronic pain and movement disorders. Powered wirelessly from outside the body, the seed-sized technology has shown promising results in early testing.

articles.title: Screen time not consistently tied to children’s emotional or behavioral problems in a large Scottish study
articles.summary: How much time children spend on screens may matter less than many assume. In a Scottish study following thousands of children to age 15, screen time showed few consistent links with emotional and behavioral difficulties.

articles.title: Family background may explain much of the mental health gap tied to sexual orientation, twin studies suggest
articles.summary: Gay, lesbian, and bisexual people report worse mental health on average than heterosexual people. But when they’re compared with their own heterosexual siblings and twins, much of that gap shrinks, a new meta-analysis of 17 studies finds.

articles.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
articles.summary: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

articles.title: Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health
articles.summary: A large study suggests loneliness and social isolation can cost people years of healthy life, especially when it comes to mental health. Men experiencing both lost about 5.8 years free from depression and anxiety, while women lost roughly 3.7 years.

articles.title: Belief in supernatural evil is linked to blaming the system for poverty
articles.summary: People who believe in the devil and hell are more likely to blame society for poverty, while those who believe in a supportive deity are less likely to do so, according to a recent survey of South Korean adults.

articles.title: Does voting by mail make for better choices? A 2020 election study suggests it might
articles.summary: Mail-in ballots are usually discussed as a way to boost turnout. New research suggests they may also help voters make better choices, with mail voters more likely to pick the candidate aligned with their stated preferences.
